summary: Describes the data plane of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP). LISP uses two namespaces, Endpoint Identifiers for hosts and Routing Locators for network attachment points, and routers exchange encapsulated packets based on them to build overlay networks. It obsoletes RFC 6830. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Each person has a name, and where they live changes. LISP wraps a letter for a name in an envelope with the current street address so it still finds them.

subtitle: How LISP routers wrap ordinary packets in UDP so that a host's identity and its network location can be kept apart.

tldr.problem: An IP address is used both as the name of a host and as the place it is attached to the network, which ties a host's identity to its topology.
tldr.mechanism: LISP splits addresses into Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) and Routing Locators (RLOCs). Tunnel routers look up the RLOC for a destination EID in a Map-Cache and wrap each packet in an outer IP, UDP and 8-octet LISP header, sent to UDP port 4341.
tldr.outcome: Hosts and underlay routers need no changes, and the design offers traffic engineering, multihoming and mobility. RFC 9300 obsoletes RFC 6830 and is a Standards Track document.

today: RFC 9300 is a Standards Track document published in October 2022 and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 6830, and it is used together with the control plane in RFC 9301.

sections.title: Separating Identity from Location
sections.content:
RFC 9300 describes the data plane of the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP). LISP is an encapsulation protocol built on one idea: the topological location of a network attachment point should be separate from the identity of the node.

That creates two namespaces. Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) identify end hosts, such as nodes or virtual machines. Routing Locators (RLOCs) are routable addresses that identify network attachment points. LISP defines the mapping between the two and the encapsulation that carries traffic from non-routable EIDs across a network that routes on RLOCs. The tunneling is dynamic, so no static provisioning is needed.

This document covers only the data plane. The control plane, which fills in the mappings, is in RFC 9301, and the architecture is in RFC 9299. LISP requires no change to host protocol stacks or underlay routers. It was first motivated by the IAB Routing and Addressing Workshop of October 2006, and it was developed to address Internet-wide route scaling, though the RFC notes that many other uses have since been found.
sections.eli5: Who you are and where you live are two different things. LISP keeps a list of both, so friends can still reach you after you move.

sections.title: EIDs, RLOCs and Tunnel Routers
sections.content:
Hosts behave exactly as they do without LISP. They send packets to destination addresses, and in LISP terms those addresses are EIDs. Routers in the middle keep forwarding on destination addresses; between the ITR and the ETR that address is an RLOC.

The work is done by Tunnel Routers. An Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) takes a packet from a site-side host, treats its destination as an EID, looks up the mapping, and prepends an outer header whose source is one of its own RLOCs and whose destination is the RLOC from the lookup. An Egress Tunnel Router (ETR) accepts packets addressed to one of its RLOCs, strips the outer header and forwards the inner packet. An xTR is a router acting as either. Related roles are the Proxy-ITR and Proxy-ETR for sites that do not run LISP, and the Re-encapsulating Tunneling Router, which acts as an ETR and then an ITR.

Some rules govern how the two spaces are used. An EID that identifies a router as a host MUST NOT be used as an RLOC, since an EID is only routable within the scope of a site. It is RECOMMENDED that a packet carries at most two LISP headers, one for separating location from identity at a site and a second inside a provider for traffic engineering.
sections.eli5: A mail room worker at your school puts each letter inside a bigger envelope with the right city address. At the other end another worker opens the big envelope and hands over the letter.

sections.title: How a Packet Finds Its Way
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an example in which host1.abc.example.com opens a TCP connection to host2.xyz.example.com. The host does a normal DNS lookup, and the address returned is the destination EID. The packet travels through the site as ordinary IP until it reaches an ITR.

The ITR must map that EID to an RLOC of an ETR at the destination site. One method is a LISP Map-Request, defined in RFC 9301, which the Mapping System helps forward to the right ETR. The ETR matches the destination EID against its configured EID-to-RLOC database. If nothing matches, the Map-Request is dropped; otherwise it returns a Map-Reply. The ITR stores the result in its Map-Cache, an on-demand cache that it manages to fit its resources.

Later packets get a LISP header addressed to the learned RLOC. The ETR receives them because the outer destination is its own address, checks the addresses, strips the header and delivers the packet. An ETR MAY also create a glean mapping from the source EID and source RLOC of a received packet, to avoid a lookup in the reverse direction.
sections.eli5: The first time, the mail room asks a directory where to send the letter and writes the answer in a notebook. After that it just reads the notebook.

sections.title: The LISP Encapsulation Header
sections.content:
An encapsulated packet is the outer IP header, a UDP header, an 8-octet LISP header, and then the original packet. The outer UDP destination port MUST be the IANA-assigned 4341, and the source port is chosen by the ITR from a hash of the inner header. All four combinations of IPv4 and IPv6 EIDs and RLOCs MUST be supported.

The first byte of the LISP header holds flag bits. N says a 24-bit nonce is present. L says Locator-Status-Bits are in use. E requests an echoed nonce. V says Map-Version numbers are present. I says an Instance ID is present, which shrinks the Locator-Status-Bits field to 8 bits. R is reserved and MUST be 0 on transmit. The two KK bits are 00 when the packet is not encrypted. The N and V bits MUST NOT both be set.

The UDP checksum SHOULD be sent as zero, and an ETR MUST accept a packet with a zero checksum. On encapsulation the outer Time to Live and DSCP SHOULD be copied from the inner header. On decapsulation the inner TTL MUST be copied from the outer when the outer value is lower, which stops the inner value rising across encapsulation cycles. ECN handling follows RFC 6040.

Instance IDs support cases such as overlapping addresses, traffic isolation and multi-tenant virtualization. An ITR copies a 24-bit value into the header and the ETR uses it to pick the forwarding table. The RFC warns that the Instance ID is not protected, so an on-path attacker can modify it.
sections.eli5: The outer envelope has a small label with switches on it that tell the receiver which extra notes are inside. The envelope always goes to the same mailbox number, 4341.

sections.title: Map-Cache and Large Packets
sections.content:
ITRs and PITRs keep the Map-Cache, which maps EID-Prefixes to Locator-Sets. A lookup is a longest-prefix match. If it fails, the router uses the control plane to fetch the mapping, and while waiting it can either drop or buffer packets. The RFC makes no recommendation. Entries expire according to their Time to Live.

Encapsulation makes packets bigger, so they can exceed the path MTU. The RFC offers two mechanisms and leaves the choice to the implementor.

  • Stateless: define H as the size of the outer headers, L as the largest packet the ITR can send without fragmentation, and S = L - H. If an encapsulated packet would exceed L and the host left the DF bit at 0, the ITR splits it into two equal fragments and encapsulates each. If DF is 1 or the packet is IPv6, it drops the packet and sends ICMPv4 Fragmentation Needed or ICMPv6 Packet Too Big with the value S. It is RECOMMENDED that L be 1500.
  • Stateful: the ITR remembers an effective MTU per Locator in each Map-Cache entry, learned from ICMP messages, and tells sources about oversized packets itself. This avoids making the destination host reassemble fragments.

With IPv4 outer headers, an implementation SHOULD set the DF bit to 1 so that ETR reassembly can be avoided.
sections.eli5: Putting a letter inside a bigger envelope can make it too fat for the mail slot. Either you cut the letter in two halves, or you remember how fat a letter each slot allows.

sections.title: Choosing and Checking RLOCs
sections.content:
A mapping returns a Locator-Set, and each RLOC has a Priority and a Weight. The RLOC with the lowest Priority is used, and Priority 255 means the RLOC MUST NOT be used for forwarding. Among equal Priorities, Weight says how to share traffic. A Weight of zero lets the client side decide the split. The server side therefore controls the list, and the client side may use others only if the list is unreachable.

For load sharing, an ITR MAY hash the source and destination addresses, or the usual 5-tuple, divide by the number of Locators and use the remainder as an index. The outer UDP source port should come from such a hash and stay the same for a flow, so core routers using link aggregation see different flows rather than one.

The RFC defines data plane ways to learn whether an RLOC is up. Locator-Status-Bits let an ITR tell an ETR which RLOCs at its site are up. The Echo-Nonce algorithm has an ITR set the N and E bits and a 24-bit nonce, and treats a missing echo as a sign that the path is down. Many implementations do not advertise Echo-Nonce support, so RLOC-Probing tends to be used. Mappings can be refreshed with Locator-Status-Bits, with a recommended 5-minute 'use-LSB' timer, or with Database Map-Versioning, specified in RFC 9302.

Gleaned entries are RECOMMENDED to be kept for only 3 seconds, pending a verifying Map-Request.
sections.eli5: Each way to reach a friend has a rank and a share. You use the best rank first, split your mail by share, and have a few tricks to check that a route still works.

sections.title: Where LISP Is Safe to Use
sections.content:
Several data plane mechanisms are meant for controlled, trusted environments. On the public Internet an xTR MUST set the N, L, E and V bits to zero, MUST NOT use Locator-Status-Bits or Echo-Nonce for reachability, and MUST NOT use gleaning, Locator-Status-Bits or Map-Versioning to update mappings. It must rely on the control plane instead.

The risks are spoofing ones. An off-path attacker can spoof a source EID or RLOC to poison a gleaned mapping or redirect traffic at a victim. The reachability bits and nonces can be manipulated to report false RLOC status, and a forged Map-Version field can force excessive signaling between xTRs. The RFC suggests Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (BCP 84) against RLOC spoofing, and a LISP-specific check of the Mapping System when decapsulating.

Where IPv6 outer fragments are allowed, ETRs, RTRs and PETRs should limit fragments awaiting reassembly to avoid a denial-of-service vector.
sections.eli5: The shortcuts only work when everyone in the club is honest. In the open world someone could fake a return address, so you should check with the directory instead.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 6830
sections.content:
RFC 9300 obsoletes RFC 6830, and most of the shortening comes from moving the control plane messaging and procedures into RFC 9301. The data plane is not backwards compatible with RFC 6830, and it has no explicit version field for future changes.

  • The limit of exactly two LISP headers is no longer mandated, though two is still RECOMMENDED.
  • The three reserved flag bits were allocated for RFC 8061. Two of them are now the KK bits, a key identifier, and one stays reserved.
  • Data plane gleaning of Map-Cache entries is now optional.

New data plane capabilities can be advertised by an ETR through the control plane using new LISP Canonical Address Format types.
